title: Welcome to the 'Show Me' era - a16z crypto
gist: Crypto's communications environment has shifted from promissory whitepaper-and-vision pitches to a 'proof stack' era demanding hard data, real partnerships, and organic user traction, driven by TradFi's entry at scale, AI's shipped consumer products, and looming market-structure legislation.

themes.theme: The shift from vision-led to proof-led crypto comms

insights.claim: For most of crypto's history the industry ran on promissory logic where a whitepaper and a token were enough to get press and community attention, but that dynamic has shifted to demanding demonstrated proof.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Founders and comms teams should expect whitepaper-only launches to underperform; media and community now filter for evidence over narrative.
insights.quote: The vision was the product. You could launch with just a whitepaper and a token, and the press and crypto community would meet you there.

insights.claim: The communications shift to a 'show me' era is being driven by three combined forces: growing skepticism of crypto after two decades, mass entrance of traditional financial institutions building real products (not just innovation-lab experiments), and the AI industry visibly shipping consumer-ready products.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating crypto pitches should weight comparisons against AI's proof-of-shipped-product bar, not crypto's historical whitepaper bar.

insights.claim: TradFi institutions have moved from watching or siloing crypto in innovation arms to building at scale, citing BlackRock's tokenization push under Larry Fink, Fidelity's custody and ETF infrastructure, JP Morgan's Onyx network, and Franklin Templeton's onchain money market fund as evidence these are now real products with institutional compliance frameworks and balance sheets behind them.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Track these institutions' onchain product rollouts as the new baseline TradFi credibility bar that crypto-native projects will be measured against.
insights.quote: These aren’t experiments anymore — they’re real products, with the corresponding TradFi compliance frameworks, institutional clients, and balance sheets behind them.

insights.claim: When the world's largest asset manager tokenizes treasuries, the credibility bar that any crypto project must clear with media, partners, and the market rises correspondingly.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Expect due-diligence and PR standards for crypto startups to keep ratcheting upward as more mega-institutions enter with tokenized products.
insights.locator: The entry of TradFi at scale

insights.claim: Passage of the GENIUS Act stablecoin legislation and a pending Senate vote on the CLARITY Act market-structure bill are pushing crypto into mainstream policy status, and if CLARITY passes it will let founders publicly discuss what they're building with a specificity not previously possible.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Watch the CLARITY Act Senate vote as a catalyst that could unlock more specific, product-level public disclosure from crypto founders, changing the comms and possibly disclosure risk calculus.
insights.quote: If CLARITY passes, it will allow founders to publicly talk about what they’re building with a level of specificity that previously was not possible.
insights.locator: The industry has entered the mainstream

insights.claim: The default question investors, media, and partners now ask has changed from 'what are you building' to 'what have you built, and who is using it,' meaning a compelling story alone no longer moves the needle without proof.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Use this reframed question as a due-diligence filter when evaluating crypto pitches or deal flow.
insights.quote: “What have you built, and who is using it?”
insights.locator: The result is a communications environment

insights.claim: The author defines a 'proof stack' as the layer of evidence — beyond the pitch — that converts a hypothetical narrative into a credible, concrete one, and argues every crypto pitch now needs this second act.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Use 'proof stack' as a due-diligence checklist framework when screening crypto startups: partnerships, hard data, and organic product-market fit signals.
insights.quote: I call it the proof stack: the layer of evidence that transforms a hypothetical, abstract narrative into a credible, concrete one.

insights.claim: Partnership announcements are no longer credible as a standalone traction signal unless they show 'teeth' — actual integrations, deployed contracts, and named partners willing to publicly explain why they chose the company over alternatives.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Investors should discount vague 'in conversations with' partnership PR and instead demand evidence of deployed integrations and named partner rationale.
insights.quote: The partnership announcement used to be a lazy substitute for traction. Now it only works if the partnership itself is evidence of traction.

insights.claim: Credible proof now requires hard onchain data — mainnet (not testnet) transaction volumes, active wallets, revenue, and retention curves reported as concrete percentages, timeframes, and baselines rather than vague claims like 'growing fast.'
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: When evaluating a crypto project's traction claims, cross-check reported metrics against public onchain dashboards like Dune or CoinMarketCap before trusting them.
insights.quote: If your numbers don’t hold up to a Dune, CoinMarketCap, or other analytics dashboard, your story won’t hold up either.
insights.locator: This also means sharing more hard data

insights.claim: Journalists covering crypto are increasingly sophisticated and now perform their own onchain verification of a company's claimed metrics rather than taking press releases at face value.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Assume any onchain metric disclosed publicly will be independently verified by press or analysts, raising the cost of exaggeration.
insights.quote: Journalists covering this space are increasingly sophisticated; they’re doing their own onchain verification.
insights.locator: This also means sharing more hard data

insights.claim: The most credible proof of product-market fit is an organic, growing user community that existed before any PR push, rather than users generated by a launch announcement.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: When assessing product-market fit signals, weight pre-existing organic community growth far more heavily than post-launch PR-driven activity spikes.
insights.quote: I believe the clearest proof of “fit” isn’t a launch announcement — it’s an organic and growing community that existed before the PR push.

insights.claim: If a project's most enthusiastic users are its own investors or others with financial skin in the game, that is a yellow flag for authenticity of demand, whereas word-of-mouth users who found the product independently constitute a genuinely credible story.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Screen a project's visible user/community base for investor and insider concentration as a red flag before crediting claimed organic traction.
insights.quote: If your most enthusiastic users are your investors, or people with skin in the game, that’s a yellow flag given they’re financially incentivized.

insights.claim: The most credible form of proof is third-party validation the company didn't manufacture itself, such as independent research, audits, and press coverage that arrived before any press push rather than because of one.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Weight unsolicited third-party coverage and independent audits more heavily than company-initiated PR when assessing legitimacy.
insights.quote: The most credible kind of proof is the kind you didn’t manufacture.

insights.claim: Early-stage founders are tempted to lead with vision because the product isn't fully formed yet, but doing so now reads as risky rather than honest in the current environment.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Advise portfolio founders to resist leading pitches with manifesto-style vision and instead sequence around concrete proof, even pre-scale.
insights.quote: But in the current environment, it reads as a risk.
insights.locator: What this means for startup comms

insights.claim: A small, concrete proof point is more persuasive than a large but abstract claim: a thousand active daily users unconnected to the founders beats a million dollars in strategic backing, and a protocol that processed $50M in volume in its first 90 days beats a protocol that will process volume once it scales.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: When comparing early-stage crypto pitches, weight small verified usage metrics over large but unproven funding or scale claims.
insights.quote: A protocol that processed $50M in volume in its first 90 days is more interesting than a protocol that “will” process volume once it scales.

insights.claim: Precision separates a thesis from a proof point: 'we're building the future of payments' is a thesis, while 'we've reduced cross-border settlement time from three days to four minutes, and here are three businesses using it today' is a proof point that carries a thesis inside it.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Use this thesis-vs-proof-point distinction as a quick litmus test when reading founder claims or pitch decks.
insights.quote: “We’re building the future of payments” is a thesis, not a proof point.
insights.locator: This also means being more precise

insights.claim: The ratio of vision to substance that crypto comms could get away with has flipped from roughly 80% vision and 20% substance in 2021 to the reverse proportion today, though vision itself remains necessary to make proof points meaningful.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Benchmark current crypto pitch decks and PR against this vision/substance ratio shift when assessing whether a project's comms style is dated.
insights.quote: you could get away with 80% vision and 20% substance back in 2021. That ratio has flipped today.

insights.claim: The author frames this shift as permanent rather than a temporary correction, arguing that the growing sophistication of crypto's media, institutional, and retail audiences has permanently raised the bar, which benefits builders with real traction because it filters out noise and makes genuine signal louder.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Treat the higher proof bar as a durable structural change in crypto fundraising and PR dynamics, not a cyclical phase to wait out.
insights.quote: The Show Me Era isn’t a temporary industry correction.
